title: Given a string, partition it so that every substring of the partition is a palindrome, and return all possible palindrome partitionings. Explain the backtracking technique that cuts the string at each position and only recurses when the prefix is a palindrome.
shortTitle: Palindrome Partitioning (All Ways to Split a String into Palindromes)

s1_definition.profdef: Palindrome Partitioning is a Subsets-pattern backtracking problem that enumerates every way to cut a string into pieces where each piece reads the same forwards and backwards. We recurse from a start index, try every end position to form a prefix, and only when that prefix is a palindrome do we add it to the current partition and recurse on the remainder. A partition is complete when the start index reaches the end of the string. The search is exponential in the worst case, bounded by the number of palindromic partitionings.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a reference token must be split into symmetric segments for a legacy validator, where every segment must read the same both ways. We want every valid way to split the token into such segments. We try cutting after the first character, after the second, and so on; whenever the piece we cut off is symmetric we accept it and recursively split what remains, otherwise we skip that cut.
s1_definition.oneliner: From each start, try every prefix, recurse only on palindromic prefixes, and record a partition when the whole string is consumed.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Palindrome Partitioning is a Subsets-pattern backtracking problem that enumerates every way to cut a string into pieces where each piece reads the same forwards and backwards. We recurse from a start index, try every end position to form a prefix, and only when that prefix is a palindrome do we add it to the current partition and recurse on the remainder. A partition is complete when the start index reaches the end of the string. The search is exponential in the worst case, bounded by the number of palindromic partitionings.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, a reference token must be split into symmetric segments for a legacy validator, where every segment must read the same both ways. We want every valid way to split the token into such segments. We try cutting after the first character, after the second, and so on; whenever the piece we cut off is symmetric we accept it and recursively split what remains, otherwise we skip that cut.

**One line to remember:** From each start, try every prefix, recurse only on palindromic prefixes, and record a partition when the whole string is consumed.

sections.s2_technical:
We recurse with a start index, a current list of pieces, and the results. If the start index equals the string length, the current list is a complete valid partition and we record a copy. Otherwise we loop the end index from start to the last character, forming the substring from start to end inclusive; if that substring is a palindrome we add it, recurse with the next start being end plus one, then remove it to backtrack.

Checking a palindrome is a simple two-pointer comparison from both ends. For example, a helper `isPalindrome(s, lo, hi)` walks inward while characters match. Only palindromic prefixes trigger recursion, which prunes the vast majority of invalid cuts early.

A senior-level nuance is that the palindrome checks can be precomputed with a dynamic-programming table so each check is constant time, turning repeated inner checks into a lookup; without it the checks add a linear factor. Another nuance is that this is subset-style exploration over cut positions, where each partitioning corresponds to a choice of where to cut.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India feeds a legacy validator that requires a reference token be broken into symmetric segments, each reading the same both ways, and operations wants every valid segmentation to test the validator. This is exactly how Palindrome Partitioning works: each segmentation is a partition into palindromic pieces.

Problem 2 — Trying every possible cut blindly would explore many invalid segmentations. This is why we only recurse when the prefix is a palindrome, pruning invalid cuts immediately and exploring only promising partitions.

The code defines a `PartitionService` exposing `palindromePartitions(token)` returning all partitionings. A `Demo` runs it over a short token and logs each partition.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: token aab.

Step 1: Start at index 0. Try the prefix a, which is a palindrome; accept it and recurse from index 1 with the current partition holding a.

Step 2: At index 1, try the prefix a, a palindrome; accept and recurse from index 2 with the partition a, a.

Step 3: At index 2, try the prefix b, a palindrome; accept and recurse from index 3. Index 3 equals the length, so record the partition a, a, b. Backtrack.

Step 4: Back at index 0, try the prefix aa, which is a palindrome; accept and recurse from index 2 with partition aa. At index 2 the prefix b is a palindrome, giving the partition aa, b. The prefix aab is not a palindrome, so it is skipped.

Step 5: The two valid partitions are a, a, b and aa, b.

```
Oct 27, 2026 9:21:05 PM com.bank.legacy.service.PartitionService backtrack
FINE: Partition [a, a, b]
FINE: Partition [aa, b]
INFO: Generated 2 palindrome partitions
INFO: NBI token 'aab' palindrome partitions: [[a, a, b], [aa, b]]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Palindrome Partitioning enumerates every way to cut a string into pieces where each piece is a palindrome. I solve it with backtracking driven by a start index. From the current start I try every end position to form a prefix, and only when that prefix is a palindrome do I accept it into the current partition and recurse on the remainder beginning just after it. When the start index reaches the end of the string the current list of pieces is a complete valid partition and I record a copy.

The key to efficiency is that I recurse only on palindromic prefixes, which prunes the enormous number of invalid cuts immediately rather than building them and rejecting them later. I check a palindrome with a simple two-pointer inward comparison, and I mention that these checks can be precomputed into a dynamic-programming table so each check becomes constant time, which matters for longer strings since the same substrings are tested repeatedly.

At the National Bank of India I used this to feed a legacy validator that required a reference token to be split into symmetric segments, generating every valid segmentation so operations could test the validator thoroughly. I backtracked over cut positions, recursed only when a prefix was a palindrome, and stored each full partition as a fresh copy. Explaining the palindrome-only recursion as the pruning mechanism, and recognising that the choice of cut positions is a subset-style exploration, is what shows an interviewer that I can apply backtracking with a correctness-driven prune to a real string-processing task.
